name: LMC
quote: Keywords: galaxies: dwarf — galaxies: interactions — galaxies: Magellanic Clouds — galaxies: structure ... Finally, these advances will help improve our general understanding of galaxy dynamics and the morphological evolution of interacting dwarf galaxies, using the MCs as a prototype for an interacting/colliding pair of galaxies.
location: Keywords; Sect. 6.3 (Constraints on the LMC–SMC Evolution), final paragraph
reader_note: Full text read (arXiv PDF v2). Galaxy label used as established throughout (keywords; 'LMC disk'; 'Magellanic-type galaxies'). The paper describes disk, off-centred bar and spiral-arm morphology and notes such structures are 'common in Magellanic Irregulars' (Sect. 1), but offers this to explain the structures by tidal interaction, not as a ground for the kind. No ground for the kind stated: N. A lenient reader might read the morphology comparison as L.

name: SMC
quote: Two massive satellites — the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds — were omitted from our study due to their large sizes, which render them impractical for a program of this scope.
location: Sect. 2 (Observations and target selection); SMC also listed in Table 2 (tertiary sample, not analysed)
reader_note: Full text read (arXiv:1806.06891v1; arXiv page lists DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/aac16b, confirming it is ApJ 860, 66, 'A MegaCam Survey of Outer Halo Satellites. III'). The SMC is not analysed: it is called a 'massive satellite' and appears only in Table 2 with compiled literature parameters. The paper never states a kind for the SMC, galaxy or cluster, and gives no ground. Coded N (no ground; here not even the label). Not X: it neither calls the SMC a cluster nor concludes its kind is undetermined.

name: Cassiopeia II
quote: The dwarf galaxy sample we focus on here comprises all the dwarf spheroidal galaxies that fall in the PAndAS footprint, as seen in Figure 1: And I, ... and the latest PAndAS discovery Cas II/And XXX. ... Cas II is reasonably faint ([value]) and has a typical size for galaxies of this luminosity ([value]).
reader_note: Full text read (arXiv PDF). The dSph label is taken as given in the sample definition, but Sect. 4.23 explicitly compares Cas II with galaxies in size at its luminosity: a comparison with the known galaxy population in light/structure (L). Borderline: the comparison is stated, not framed as an argument for the kind; a stricter reader might code N. Magnitudes and radii replaced by [value] for caution (not forbidden quantities). The same section notes its distance and systemic velocity are close to NGC 147/185 ('likely ... the same group'); grouping, not a kind ground.

name: M 32
quote: However, in addition to the dSph satellites, M31 also has a transition dwarf (LGS3), a dwarf irregular (IC10, although it is much lower luminosity than either of the Magellanic Clouds), three dwarf elliptical galaxies (NGC205, 147 and 185), a compact elliptical (M32) and a low mass spiral galaxy (M33). ... the compact elliptical M32 is a known outlier in this projection due to its extreme concentration
location: Sect. 3.2 (Membership of the M31 sub-group); Sect. 4 (discussion of Fig. 6, absolute magnitude vs half-light radius); Table 1 (type cE)
reader_note: Full text read (arXiv PDF v2). Catalogue of galaxies within 3 Mpc; M32 enters as a galaxy by catalogue inclusion with morphological type cE, no ground argued. Sect. 4 says the galaxies 'seem well separated from the (Galactic) globular clusters' in magnitude vs half-light radius, but singles out M32 as an outlier from that relation, so the size-luminosity comparison is not a ground for M32. Table 5 comment 'Likely significant age spread and gradients?' is a population note, not offered as a ground for the kind. Coded N.

name: NGC 205
quote: However, in addition to the dSph satellites, M31 also has a transition dwarf (LGS3), a dwarf irregular (IC10, although it is much lower luminosity than either of the Magellanic Clouds), three dwarf elliptical galaxies (NGC205, 147 and 185), a compact elliptical (M32) and a low mass spiral galaxy (M33).
location: Sect. 3.2 (Membership of the M31 sub-group); Table 1 (type dE/dSph)
reader_note: Full text read (arXiv PDF v2). Catalogue inclusion with morphological type dE/dSph; no ground for the kind argued. Table 4 comment reports an HI velocity gradient for NGC 205 (i.e. gas is detected), but as a kinematic note, not offered as a ground for the kind; a lenient reader might code G. Coded N.

name: Carina III
quote: By simultaneously modeling the spatial and the color-magnitude stellar distributions, we find that both Carina II and Carina III are likely dwarf galaxies, although this is less clear for Carina III. ... Both satellites lie in a region of size-luminosity space occupied by the ultra-faint dwarfs, close to the detection limit of current surveys. ... both Carinas appears to be much too diffuse to be globular clusters, although for Car III, its smaller physical size may actually be consistent with the hypothesis of a disrupting globular cluster.
location: Abstract; Sect. 5 Discussion and conclusions (Figure 6 paragraph)
reader_note: First naming is the discovery paper itself (arXiv v1 22 Jan 2018; only version). Hedged label ('likely dwarf galaxies', 'less clear for Carina III') adopted by the paper; ground is size-luminosity comparison with ultra-faint dwarfs and globular clusters (L). The paper also states the cluster alternative remains viable for Car III and that kinematics/metallicities must decide; a reader applying D-049 item 1 strictly should note this is a hedge, not a conclusion that the kind is undetermined.

name: Draco II
quote: Since the beginning of 2015, a combination of new optical imaging surveys and a re-analysis of SDSS data resulted in the detection of fourteen additional Milky Way companions tentatively classified as dwarf galaxies (... Laevens et al. 2015b). ... The provisional classification of these stellar systems as dwarf galaxies relies on their low surface brightnesses, large physical sizes, large ellipticities, and/or large heliocentric distances. ... Other recently reported dwarf galaxy candidates (green diamonds) include Hydra II (Martin et al. 2015), Triangulum II (Laevens et al. 2015a), Pegasus III (Kim et al. 2015a), Draco II and Sagittarius II (Laevens et al. 2015b).
location: Sect. 1 Introduction; Fig. 1 caption (five candidates outside the DES footprint); Fig. 4 caption
reader_note: arXiv v1 14 Aug 2015. Collective naming: Draco II is named as a 'dwarf galaxy candidate' and plotted with the galaxy candidates, separately from the 'systems of ambiguous classification' (which include Laevens 3 from the same discovery paper). The ground (L) is stated for the group, not argued for Draco II individually; a stricter reader could code N. Note the paper attributes the dwarf-galaxy classification to Laevens et al. 2015b, which itself left Draco II's kind open.

name: Horologium I
quote: Koposov et al. [43] report 9 new objects. One of these, Reticulum 2 (Ret2), ... is the nearest dwarf galaxy after Segue 1 ... Gray curves correspond to the collection of dwarfs used in [41] as well as the 8 other newly discovered DES dwarfs.
reader_note: arXiv v1 8 Mar 2015 (one day before Bechtol et al. 2015, arXiv:1503.02584, 9 Mar 2015). Collective, unnamed naming: 'the 8 other newly discovered DES dwarfs' are the other eight of Koposov et al.'s nine objects, which include Horologium 1; they are treated as dwarf-galaxy targets in the gamma-ray analysis. No ground stated. UNCERTAIN: if a naming must refer to the system by name, the first naming is Bechtol et al. 2015 (9 Mar 2015), 'Its Plummer radius of ~60 pc establishes it as a likely dwarf galaxy, twice as extended as the largest globular clusters with comparable luminosities' (L). Both are 2015.

name: Phoenix II
quote: Koposov et al. [43] report 9 new objects. One of these, Reticulum 2 (Ret2), ... is the nearest dwarf galaxy after Segue 1 ... Gray curves correspond to the collection of dwarfs used in [41] as well as the 8 other newly discovered DES dwarfs.
reader_note: arXiv v1 8 Mar 2015. Collective, unnamed naming of Koposov et al.'s other eight objects (which include Phoenix 2) as 'DES dwarfs', treated as dwarf-galaxy targets. No ground stated. UNCERTAIN: the earliest by-name candidates are Bechtol et al. 2015 (9 Mar; 'dwarf galaxy candidates' collectively, but for Phoenix II 'we cannot draw firm conclusions on its nature', already coded X on the sheet) and Drlica-Wagner et al. 2015 Fermi-LAT/DES (arXiv:1503.02632, 9 Mar; 'DES Dwarf Spheroidal Galaxy Candidates', DES J2339.9-5424 listed by name; no ground for the label stated in the passages read). All are 2015 and none gives L, P or G specifically for Phoenix II.

name: Reticulum II
quote: We present a search for γ-ray emission from the direction of the newly discovered dwarf galaxy Reticulum 2. ... Koposov et al. [43] report 9 new objects. One of these, Reticulum 2 (Ret2), at a distance of 30 kpc, is the nearest dwarf galaxy after Segue 1 (Seg1, 23 kpc) and Sagittarius (24 kpc).
location: Title ('Evidence for Gamma-ray Emission from the Newly Discovered Dwarf Galaxy Reticulum 2', v1); Abstract; Introduction (para. 2)
reader_note: arXiv v1 8 Mar 2015, between Koposov et al. 2015 (6 Mar; 'ultra-faint satellite', kind left open) and Bechtol et al. 2015 (9 Mar; 'almost certainly a dwarf galaxy', L). Label used without a stated ground; the only property cited is relative luminosity, used to argue for a larger halo, not for the kind. Same publication year (2015) as Koposov et al. 2015.

name: Reticulum III
quote: Like DES J2204−4626, DES J0345−6026 can be tentatively classified as a dwarf galaxy based on its physical size and low surface brightness.
location: Sect. 6.1 Review of Individual Candidates (Reticulum III); title 'Eight Ultra-faint Galaxy Candidates ...'
reader_note: First naming is the discovery paper itself (arXiv v1 14 Aug 2015; same sentence in v1 and v2). Hedged ('tentatively') label adopted by the paper on size and surface brightness (L). The paper also says spectroscopy is needed to classify definitively.

name: Segue 1
quote: Fig. 1.— Stellar profiles of the dwarf galaxies. ... even in poorly sampled satellites such as e.g. BooII, LeoT or Seg1 that all contain less than 100 stars. ... Many SDSS satellites are in fact smaller that 100 pc (BooII, CVnII, Com, SDSSJ1058+2843, Seg1 and Wil1). Therefore, it might appear more difficult to assign these systems to one population or the other. However, spectroscopic surveys conducted so far (Martin et al. 2007; Simon & Geha 2007) show that they are dark matter dominated (except maybe for SDSSJ1058+2843 and Seg1 for which no spectroscopic data have yet been published). ... This somewhat arbitrary threshold was used as it divides the complete MW dwarf galaxy sample in two subsamples of similar sizes (10 and 11 members).
location: Fig. 1 caption; Sect. 5 (Figure 6 discussion); footnote 13 (v1, 19 May 2008)
reader_note: Martin, de Jong & Rix 2008. Collective naming: Seg1 is profiled in the figure of 'the dwarf galaxies' and counted in the 'complete MW dwarf galaxy sample'. No ground given for Seg1: the dynamical argument is stated for the group but explicitly excludes Seg1, and the size discussion says assignment is 'more difficult'. UNCERTAIN: the paper hedges and does not argue the label. Earliest explicit by-name naming found: Tollerud et al. 2008 (arXiv:0806.4381, 26 Jun 2008), 'we will at most see a galaxy like Segue 1', table ground stated as large mass-to-light ratios (D). Then Geha et al. 2009 (arXiv:0809.2781, Sep 2008), D. None gives L, P or G.

name: Segue 2
quote: Under the simple assumption of an isothermal halo, the current circular velocity of Segue 2 is vcirc ∼ [value]. The original vcirc before the tiny dwarf accreted onto the Milky Way halo as part of a parent subgroup might have been close to [value] ... Initial halo masses corresponding to such circular velocities are below [value].
location: Sect. 5 Conclusions (Satellites of Satellites); keywords 'galaxies: dwarf - galaxies: individual (Segue 2)'
reader_note: Discovery paper (arXiv v1 4 Mar 2009). The paper calls Segue 2 'the tiny dwarf' only in a dynamical (circular velocity, halo mass) argument; it elsewhere calls it a 'satellite', notes its half-light radius is 'small compared to typical ultrafaint dwarf galaxies', and its introduction leaves the kind of its analogues (Coma, Segue 1, Boo II) open. UNCERTAIN whether 'dwarf' alone counts as a galaxy label. If not, the next naming found is Walker et al. 2009 (arXiv:0906.0341, 1 Jun 2009), which lists Segue 2 in its table of 'dSph Structural Parameters, Velocity Dispersions and Estimated Masses' (D). Either way D.

name: Triangulum II
quote: The recent discovery of ten new dwarf galaxy candidates by the Dark Energy Survey (DES) and the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (Pan-STARRS) ... Shortly thereafter, yet another dwarf candidate (Triangulum II) was discovered from within the data from the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (Pan-STARRS) [25]. ... Of particular interest are the new dwarf candidates Reticulum II and Triangulum II, which are each located at a distance of only ∼30 kpc from Earth, making them promising targets for dark matter searches.
location: Abstract; Sect. I Introduction; Table I caption ('the new Pan-STARRS dwarf candidate'); Sect. VII Summary and conclusions
reader_note: Hooper & Linden 2015, arXiv v1 20 Mar 2015, two days after the discovery paper (Laevens et al. 2015a, 18 Mar 2015, which stayed agnostic). Hedged label ('dwarf candidate', 'dwarf galaxy candidates') adopted; Triangulum II is analysed as a dwarf-galaxy target. A size argument is given for Reticulum II only; no ground is stated for Triangulum II. Distance is cited only as a reason it is a good gamma-ray target.

name: Ursa Major II
quote: Based on its extent and its stellar population, we argue that this is a previously unknown satellite galaxy of the Milky Way ... Based on its spatial extent (∼ 0.5◦ × 0.25◦ , or ∼ 250 × 125 pc at a heliocentric distance of ∼ 30 kpc, see §3), its CMD morphology (see §3), and its extremely low surface brightness, we conclude that this is most likely a hitherto unknown dSph galaxy. ... Additionally, the CMD does not resemble that of a single stellar population, as expected for a typical globular cluster.
location: Abstract; Sect. 2 Data and discovery (v1, 26 Jun 2006)
reader_note: First naming is a discovery paper (Zucker et al. 2006). The other discovery paper, Grillmair 2006 (arXiv:astro-ph/0605396, 16 May 2006), is earlier but calls the object 'a new globular cluster or dwarf galaxy' and does not adopt the galaxy label. Belokurov et al. 2007 Orphan stream (astro-ph/0605705, v1 29 May 2006) was checked: its v1 abstract does not mention the object and its v1 PDF is not available on arXiv; the v2 text naming UMa II cites Zucker et al. 2006, so it is not earlier. Same year (2006) as Grillmair 2006.

name: Andromeda XV
quote: Two new relatively luminous (MV ∼ −9) dwarf galaxies And XV and XVI are found in the study ... we discuss briefly here two new dwarf galaxies which were discovered immediately from simple visual inspection of the starcounts maps. ... It is also curious that And XV appears to be structurally disturbed and elongated, which is suggestive of the action of galactic tides. Yet how this very distant galaxy might have been affected by tides is hard to imagine.
location: Abstract; Sect. 6.1 Discovery of 2 bright satellites; Sect. 11 Conclusions
reader_note: First naming is the discovery paper itself (arXiv v1 10 Apr 2007). The label is used from the start; luminosity, distance and profile fits are reported, but the paper gives no argument for why it is a galaxy rather than a cluster. Borderline L/N; coded N because no ground is stated. Conclusions add 'Follow-up studies are currently underway to understand the nature of these objects'.
